events.ai_basis: The construction in Theorem 1.3 is a generalisation of the one presented at the beginning of the Introduction and was generated by ChatGPT 5.4, which also gave a correct but rather long proof.

why: The statement is universal over even orders and demands every pair of 1-factors be Hamiltonian. Kotzig (n−1 prime) and Anderson (n/2 prime) settle infinite families of orders, so they are cases; isolated orders (Dinitz–Stinson, Wolfe K_52, Pike K_56) and the K_16 enumeration are finitely many instances of the universal statement; a second factorisation at already-covered orders and the stale data table settle nothing new. Glock–Sgueglia (random graphs, k matchings) and Allsop–Wanless (bipartite K_{11,11}) answer changed questions. The close call is Cheng–Sgueglia: it does not settle any order, but it raises the proportion of pairwise-perfect 1-factors achievable in a 1-factorisation of K_n to 1−o(1) for all large even n. I read that as moving a proportion on a still-open question (bound) rather than as a variant, since the quantity it moves is the one the conjecture wants to equal all n−1 factors. On AI, the authors say ChatGPT 5.4 generated the Theorem 1.3 construction, which Theorem 1.2 is built on. That construction is mathematics in the result, even though the humans re-proved it and wrote the Theorem 1.2 argument themselves, so the event is assisted, not generated.
doubts: Bound versus variant for Cheng–Sgueglia is arguable: it could be read as a weaker form of the conjecture, and on that reading it would be discarded. The AI quote comes through a fetch summary, not raw source text. Dinitz–Stinson's list of orders rests on OCR'd snippets. Pre-snapshot verification calls rely on journal publication cited from snippets.
